newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.N. envoy in Rwanda for talks on U.N. resolution.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy in Rwanda for talks on U.N. resolution.

text.p: A U.N. special envoy arrived in Rwanda on Wednesday but Kigali said a U.N. resolution calling for a ceasefire in Zaire was "absurd" because it failed to take into account rebel views.
Mohamed Sahnoun, the first joint envoy of the United Nations and Organisation of African Unity, said on arrival in Kigali he had to meet all the protagonists in the eastern Zaire conflict.
But he avoided directly saying whether he would meet rebel leader Laurent Kabila and U.N. officials declined to outline his programme after his talks with government leaders in Kigali.
Asked whether he would meet Kabila, Sahnoun told reporters: "In the kind of mission I am undertaking, I will have to see all the protagonists, I cannot exclude any party to the conflict."
"...I'm not ruling out meeting any person or representative whom I feel is involved in a solution of the crisis," he added.
The U.N. Security Council in a resolution called on Tuesday for an immediate ceasefire in the central African state as part of a five-point U.N. peace plan after a request from Sahnoun.

The five-point plan included an immediate ceasefire, the withdrawal of all foreign forces, including mercenaries, respect for the territorial integrity of Zaire and a peaceful settlement through dialogue and convening of an international conference.
Sahnoun, who flew in to Kigali from talks in Kinshasa, said he had discussed parts of the substance of the resolution with Zairean leaders and there were signs of a positive reaction.
But Claude Dusaidi, political adviser to Rwandan strongman Vice-President Paul Kagame, told Reuters the Security Council had started on the "wrong footing" by failing to first consult the rebels.

"This is clearly absurd because even if neighbours like us agree to the proposals, they would be useless without the agreement or consent of the rebel group," he added before Sahnoun met Kagame and Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu.
Dusaidi criticised Sahnoun for sending recommendations to the council without consulting all parties to the conflict.
Burundi welcomed the five-point U.N. peace plan but, like Rwanda and Uganda, again rejected Zairean government accusations their troops were fighting alongside the Rwandan-backed rebels.
Zaire criticised the resolution as "too timid" for not condemning the alleged intervention of neighbours in the war.
Asked about the Zairean accusations of Rwandan direct involvement in eastern Zaire, Sahnoun said the Security Council had to investigate and verify such charges before taking any decision.

Dusaidi said that Rwanda would have supported a resolution calling for an immediate ceasefire and direct talks between the Zairean government and the rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) led by Kabila.
The rebels have seized a stretch of eastern Zaire at least 1,000-km (600 miles) long bordering on Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania since the start of their revolt last October.
Sahnoun was appointed last month as U.N. special envoy to bring peace to the Great Lakes region of central Africa.
He resigned as special representative to Somalia in 1992 after then U.N. secretary-general Boutros Boutros-Ghali rebuked him for saying the U.N. was slow to react to famine in the country.
